title: How to catch fake expenses with one digit
description:
Look only at the first digit of every expense. In honest books about 30% start with a 1 and under 5% with a 9, because money grows by percent: getting from 100 to 200 means doubling, but from 900 to 1,000 is only 11% more, so amounts sit on 1 far longer. In this example the approval limit is $5,000, and one clerk's claims start with a 4 almost a third of the time instead of under 10%: dozens of claims just under the limit. That's Benford's law; Simon Newcomb noticed it in 1881, and auditors and tax agencies use it to choose which transactions to check. It only works for amounts that span several orders of magnitude, not things like heights.

Numbers checked in code (exact log10 probabilities, 200,000 simulated expenses, 10,000 simulated clerks). Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benford%27s_law and https://www.lawtimesnews.com/news/features/focus-benfords-law-a-key-weapon-for-detecting-fraud/261374

facts_checked: Simulated honest books (200,000 log-uniform and lognormal amounts): 30% start with 1, 5% with 9 (verify.py)
Applies when values span several orders of magnitude; fails for height, weight (Wikipedia)
Example clerk: 150 honest + 50 claims at $4,800-4,999 -> 32% start with 4 ('almost a third'); 10,000 simulated clerks 32.3%; honest clerk chance < 1e-18 (verify.py)

Fraudsters structure amounts just under scrutiny thresholds; Benford's law used by external auditors and the Canada Revenue Agency to narrow which transactions to check (https://www.lawtimesnews.com/news/features/focus-benfords-law-a-key-weapon-for-detecting-fraud/261374)
Simon Newcomb noticed it in 1881 from worn logarithm-table pages (Wikipedia)
CTA answer: about 18% of honest amounts start with 2 (verify.py)

beats.say: You're a fraud investigator, and someone at this company is faking expenses. Here's how you catch them.
Ignore the amounts. Write down only the first digit of each one. 1,280 dollars? That's a 1.
Count them. In honest books, about 30% start with a 1. Only about 5% start with a 9.
Money grows by percent. To get from 100 to 200, it has to double. From 900 to 1,000, it only needs 11% more. So amounts sit on 1 far longer.
It works when amounts run from tens to thousands, like expenses do.
Now, your company's approval limit is 5,000 dollars. Anything above it needs a manager.
Check one clerk. Almost a third of their expenses start with a 4. Honest books: under 10%.
Zoom in. 4,850. 4,920. 4,975. Every one sits just under the limit.
Uh-oh. You have 10,000 expenses and no time. You don't need it. The digits point to one clerk and 50 claims.
And there you have it: one digit caught them, and you never opened the other 9,950 receipts.
This is Benford's law. Simon Newcomb noticed it in 1881, and auditors still use it today.
